beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output.
beats.got: Reading what the agent says doesn't tell you whether it's safe, so you need a separate check.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: nothing new; homework links I haven't opened.

beats.trigger: **Evaluate** residual risk: what is left, and what future sessions need before touching the system
beats.got: A verb list, like every training slide. Residual risk is the only phrase that sounded like real risk work.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I'm asked to think about what I'd check before I trust it. That's a fair question.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent writes text and the harness turns it into an action. I can ask it myself and check, so I don't have to take anyone's word for it.

beats.trigger: Agent systems do not offer certainty.
beats.got: The slide admits up front that nobody can promise this is safe.

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: Old security assumed the software did the same thing every time. I knew that already.

beats.trigger: The dangerous move is getting your agent to *decide* to do something harmful with access it has, through well-formed English in a document it reads.
beats.got: The attack is a plain sentence in a document the agent reads, and it can talk the agent into misusing access it already has. Firewalls don't help against that. This is different from the last three programmes.

beats.trigger: Pick one risk and apply the smallest change that reduces it.
beats.got: A loop of assess, mitigate, reassess. It reads like a risk-register method I've seen before, but the five mitigations are concrete.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer.
beats.got: You're allowed to write down that you don't know, and closing that gap takes evidence. I wish more steering groups worked that way.

beats.trigger: Scope it down far enough and the system is safe and useless.
beats.got: Safety and usefulness pull against each other, and someone has to sign for where the line sits.

beats.trigger: Expect it to cost you a feature.
beats.got: The safest mitigation is not connecting the thing, and it costs a feature. Nobody sells it like that.

beats.trigger: The discipline is what carries.
beats.got: The complexity is admitted, but this closing slide has the mantra tone I'm tired of.

beats.trigger: a skill is a reusable check you run again instead of re-prompting from memory.
beats.got: A skill is a saved check I can rerun. It's like a checklist the agent loads.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The agent ran our policy text against my system and sorted what it could check from what it couldn't. That I can test, so I'll look at the rows.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.
beats.got: I tell it what actually matters here and it reshapes the check. A generic brochure doesn't help anyone.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: Twenty-two minutes of the agent asking me questions to build one skill with a policy lens and an agent-risk lens.

beats.trigger: "You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."
beats.got: I answer what I know and hand the rest to the agent. I check that all four risk patterns are in the result.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: Install steps and an ls to confirm the file is there. Admin.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The skill is a rerunnable check and our existing controls stay. Good, nobody gets to skip IT.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The exercise isn't meant to give me a clean pass. It's meant to run the loop once.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: I check the skill shows up.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The check can find things I missed and also tell me what I thought was settled isn't. I can open the report and judge that myself.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: Seeing the ranked risks in my own system is meant to be uncomfortable, and I'm supposed to trust that feeling. Fair, if a bit staged.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected.
beats.got: I fixed one risk, ran the check again, and what's left is written down and accepted on record. A tidy result would have made me suspicious.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report.
beats.got: When I'm stuck I take the report and one narrow question to legal or security instead of arguing with the agent.

beats.trigger: We did this for one risk.
beats.got: One risk is the demo. Doing it for every risk is the actual work, and the course says so plainly.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent.
beats.got: A recap. 'Recipe 4' sounds like a cookbook, but the substance holds.

beats.trigger: The unease stays.
beats.got: The agent writes a few rules into the instructions file for future sessions, and I'm told to push back where it's wrong.

beats.trigger: A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.
beats.got: Skills can be shared with a teammate. Fine, and it's said modestly.

beats.trigger: Well-formed English is the attack surface, even via sources.
beats.got: A short recap, and the attack-surface line is the one I'd keep.

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors.
beats.got: Homework with a mild nudge. I'll probably skip it.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real cases, a court filing and a consultancy report, with a question about the missing check. Those I might read.

take_homes: The attack on an agent is ordinary text in a document it reads. A firewall won't stop that.
You never get certainty. You write down what risk is left, who accepted it, and 'I can't tell' counts as an answer.
The cheapest fix is not opening a door, and it costs you a feature.

monday.move: Ask whoever owns our first agent pilot what the agent can read and write, and what we have written down about what is left over.
monday.who: The pilot owner, and legal if the answer is vague
monday.stop_condition: If the answer is only a slide or a promise, with no report I can open
monday.blocker: A calendar full of the last programme's steering groups, and I don't have a pilot of my own to run this on.

misconception.why: The old programmes never said where they'd fail. This one says outright that certainty isn't on offer and that closing a door costs a feature, and I can run the check on a real system and read the output. I still think plenty of this is 'wait and see'. The security part just isn't the same slide deck.

one_line: Less hype than I expected: it says you can't be certain, shows you how to find what's left, and the 'close a door, lose a feature' point is honest.
